reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: An immune-mediated disorder of central nervous system inhibition characterised by progressive axial and proximal muscle rigidity with superimposed painful spasms
Rigidity typically involves the trunk and abdominal wall, producing an exaggerated lumbar lordosis and a stiff, board-like posture
Spasms are often triggered by startle, emotional stress, or sudden movement and can be severe enough to cause falls or fractures
Most cases are associated with high-titre antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65); a smaller subset relate to antibodies against amphiphysin or glycine receptors
It commonly coexists with other autoimmune conditions, particularly type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease, and pernicious anaemia
A paraneoplastic form, often linked to amphiphysin antibodies and breast or other tumours, should be considered especially with atypical or rapidly progressive disease
Electromyography characteristically shows continuous motor unit activity in agonist and antagonist muscles that persists at rest
Treatment principles combine GABA-enhancing symptomatic therapy for rigidity and spasm with immunotherapy directed at the underlying autoimmune process
reference.pathophysiology: Stiff-person syndrome is thought to arise from impaired GABAergic inhibition in the central nervous system, largely on an autoimmune basis. Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase, the enzyme that synthesises the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA, or to other synaptic proteins such as glycine receptors and amphiphysin, are associated with reduced inhibitory tone in spinal and brainstem circuits. The loss of descending and segmental inhibition leads to continuous co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles, producing sustained rigidity and stimulus-sensitive spasms.
additionalDifferentials: Neuromyotonia and other peripheral hyperexcitability syndromes
Parkinsonism and progressive supranuclear palsy with axial rigidity
additionalInvestigations: Anti-GAD65 antibodies, with glycine receptor and amphiphysin antibodies when indicated
Electromyography demonstrating continuous motor unit activity
Screening for associated autoimmune disease including diabetes and thyroid disorders
Investigation for an underlying malignancy in suspected paraneoplastic cases
MRI to exclude structural spinal or cerebral causes of rigidity
redFlags: Spasms severe enough to impair breathing or cause fractures and falls
Rapid progression or atypical features suggesting a paraneoplastic cause
Autonomic instability during severe spasm episodes
New systemic symptoms prompting malignancy search
reference.prognosis: The course is usually chronic and progressive but often responsive, at least partially, to symptomatic and immunomodulatory treatment; some patients stabilise or improve, while paraneoplastic cases depend on treatment of the underlying tumour and can be more refractory.
pitfalls: Mistaking the disorder for a functional or psychiatric condition given the stress-sensitive spasms
Failing to check for associated autoimmune diseases and an occult malignancy
Overlooking the diagnostic value of anti-GAD antibodies and characteristic EMG findings
Relying on symptomatic drugs alone without considering immunotherapy
